claim: Constraint-based modelling (CBM) is a powerful tool for the analysis of evolutionary trajectories.
source: Constraint-based modelling (CBM) is a powerful tool for the analysis of evolutionary trajectories.
evidence: This is a general statement about CBM capabilities, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: The evolution of novel metabolic pathways from existing parts may be predicted using constraint-based modelling (CBM) (Orth et al., 2010).
source: The evolution of novel metabolic pathways from existing parts may be predicted using constraint-based modelling (CBM) (Orth et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Orth et al., 2010.

claim: C4 photosynthesis evolved independently in at least 67 independent origins in the plant kingdom (Scheben et al., 2017).
source: C4 photosynthesis evolved independently in at least 67 independent origins in the plant kingdom (Scheben et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Scheben et al., 2017.

claim: C4 photosynthesis allows colonisation of marginal habitats (Sage et al., 2012).
source: it allows colonisation of marginal habitats (Sage et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sage et al., 2012.

claim: C4 photosynthesis allows high biomass production in annuals such as crops (Sage, 2004; Edwards et al., 2010).
source: high biomass production in annuals such as crops (Sage, 2004; Edwards et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sage, 2004 and Edwards et al., 2010.

claim: The C4 cycle acts as a biochemical pump which enriches the CO2 concentration at the site of Rubisco to overcome a major limitation of carbon fixation (Sage, 2004).
source: The C4 cycle acts as a biochemical pump which enriches the CO2 concentration at the site of Rubisco to overcome a major limitation of carbon fixation (Sage, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sage, 2004.

claim: Rubisco can react productively with CO2 and form two molecules of 3-PGA.
source: Rubisco, the carbon fixation enzyme, can react productively with CO2 and form two molecules of 3-PGA
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about Rubisco function.

claim: Rubisco reacts with O2 and produces 2-phosphoglycolate which requires detoxification by photorespiration (Ogren and Bowes, 1971).
source: it also reacts with O2 and produces 2-phosphoglycolate which requires detoxification by photorespiration (Ogren and Bowes, 1971)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ogren and Bowes, 1971.

claim: The ratio between carboxylation and oxygenation reactions is determined by the enzyme specificity towards CO2, by the temperature, and the concentrations of both reactants.
source: The ratio between both reactions is determined by the enzyme specificity towards CO2, by the temperature, and the concentrations of both reactants
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about Rubisco kinetics.

claim: Evolution of Rubisco itself is constrained since any increase in specificity is paid for by a reduction in speed (Spreitzer and Salvucci, 2002).
source: Evolution of Rubisco itself is constrained since any increase in specificity is paid for by a reduction in speed (Spreitzer and Salvucci, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Spreitzer and Salvucci, 2002.

claim: Rubisco is a comparatively slow enzyme and can comprise up to 50% of the total leaf protein (Ellis, 1979).
source: Rubisco is a comparatively slow enzyme and can comprise up to 50% of the total leaf protein (Ellis, 1979)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ellis, 1979.

claim: In the C4 cycle, phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase affixes CO2 to a C3 acid, phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP), forming a C4 acid, oxaloacetate (OAA).
source: In the C4 cycle, phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase affixes CO2 to a C3 acid, phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP), forming a C4 acid, oxaloacetate (OAA).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C4 photosynthesis biochemistry.

claim: The C4 acid is stabilized by reduction to malate or transamination to aspartate.
source: After stabilisation of the resulting C4 acid by reduction to malate or transamination to aspartate
evidence: This is established knowledge about C4 photosynthesis biochemistry.

claim: The C4 acid is transferred to the site of Rubisco and decarboxylated by one of three possible decarboxylation enzymes: NADP-dependent malic enzyme (NADP-ME), NAD-dependent malic enzyme (NAD-ME), or PEP carboxykinase (PEP-CK) (Hatch, 1987; Schlüter et al., 2016b).
source: it is transferred to the site of Rubisco and decarboxylated by one of three possible decarboxylation enzymes, NADP-dependent malic enzyme (NADP-ME), NAD-dependent malic enzyme (NAD-ME), or PEP carboxykinase (PEP-CK) (Hatch, 1987; Schlüter et al., 2016b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hatch, 1987 and Schlüter et al., 2016b.

claim: Zea mays uses NADP-ME (Pick et al., 2011).
source: Species such as corn (Zea mays) (Pick et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pick et al., 2011.

claim: Sorghum bicolor uses NADP-ME (Döring et al., 2016).
source: great millet (Sorghum bicolor) (Döring et al., 2016) use NADP-ME
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Döring et al., 2016.

claim: Panicum miliaceum uses NAD-ME (Hatch, 1987).
source: species like common millet (Panicum miliaceum) (Hatch, 1987)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hatch, 1987.

claim: Gynandropsis gynandra uses NAD-ME (Feodorova et al., 2010; Voznesenskaya et al., 2007).
source: African spinach (Gynandropsis gynandra) (Feodorova et al., 2010; Voznesenskaya et al., 2007) use NAD-ME
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Feodorova et al., 2010 and Voznesenskaya et al., 2007.

claim: Panicum maximum uses mainly PEP-CK (Bräutigam et al., 2014).
source: species such as guinea grass (Panicum maximum) (Bräutigam et al., 2014) use mainly PEP-CK
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bräutigam et al., 2014.

claim: Mixed forms are only known to occur between a malic enzyme and PEP-CK but not between both malic enzymes (Wang et al., 2014).
source: Mixed forms are only known to occur between a malic enzyme and PEP-CK but not between both malic enzymes (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: After decarboxylation, the C3 acid diffuses back to the site of phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase (PEPC) and is recycled for another C4 cycle by pyruvate phosphate dikinase (PPDK) (Hatch, 1987; Schlüter et al., 2016b).
source: After decarboxylation, the C3 acid diffuses back to the site of phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase (PEPC) and is recycled for another C4 cycle by pyruvate phosphate dikinase (PPDK) (Hatch, 1987; Schlüter et al., 2016b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hatch, 1987 and Schlüter et al., 2016b.

claim: All the enzymes involved in the C4 cycle are also present in C3 plants (Aubry et al., 2011).
source: All the enzymes involved in the C4 cycle are also present in C3 plants (Aubry et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Aubry et al., 2011.

claim: In the most typical form of C4 photosynthesis, the C4 cycle is distributed between different cell types in a leaf in an arrangement called Kranz anatomy (Haberlandt, 1904).
source: In its most typical form, this C4 cycle is distributed between different cell types in a leaf in an arrangement called Kranz anatomy (Haberlandt, 1904).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Haberlandt, 1904.

claim: Initial carbon fixation by PEPC occurs in the mesophyll cell, the outer layer of photosynthetic tissue.
source: Initial carbon fixation by PEPC occurs in the mesophyll cell, the outer layer of photosynthetic tissue.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C4 photosynthesis anatomy.

claim: The secondary fixation by Rubisco after decarboxylation occurs in an inner layer of photosynthetic tissue, the bundle sheath which in turn surrounds the veins.
source: The secondary fixation by Rubisco after decarboxylation occurs in an inner layer of photosynthetic tissue, the bundle sheath which in turn surrounds the veins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C4 photosynthesis anatomy.

claim: Mesophyll and bundle sheath cells are connected by plasmodesmata which are pores with limited transfer specificity between cells.
source: Both cells are connected by plasmodesmata which are pores with limited transfer specificity between cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about plant cell anatomy.

claim: A model which may test possible carbon fixation pathways at the molecular level requires two cell architectures connected by transport processes (Bräutigam and Weber, 2010).
source: A model which may test possible carbon fixation pathways at the molecular level thus requires two cell architectures connected by transport processes (Bräutigam and Weber, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bräutigam and Weber, 2010.

claim: Evolution of different metabolic modes from a ground state, the metabolism of Escherichia coli, such as glycerol usage (Lewis et al., 2010) or endosymbiotic metabolism (Pál et al., 2006) have been successfully predicted.
source: Evolution of different metabolic modes from a ground state, the metabolism of Escherichia coli, such as glycerol usage (Lewis et al., 2010) or endosymbiotic metabolism (Pál et al., 2006) have been successfully predicted.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lewis et al., 2010 and Pál et al., 2006.

claim: Metabolic maps of eukaryotic metabolism are of higher complexity compared to bacteria since they require information about intracellular compartmentation and intracellular transport (Duarte, 2004).
source: Metabolic maps of eukaryotic metabolism are of higher complexity compared to bacteria since they require information about intracellular compartmentation and intracellular transport (Duarte, 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Duarte, 2004.

claim: The C4 cycle is not predicted by current C4 models unless the C4 cycle is forced by constraints (Gomes de Oliveira Dal'Molin et al., 2011; Mallmann et al., 2014).
source: The C4 cycle is not predicted by these current C4 models unless the C4 cycle is forced by constraints (Gomes de Oliveira Dal'Molin et al., 2011; Mallmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gomes de Oliveira Dal'Molin et al., 2011 and Mallmann et al., 2014.

claim: In the C4GEM model, the fluxes representing the C4 cycle are a priori constrained to the cell types (Gomes de Oliveira Dal'Molin et al., 2011).
source: In the C4GEM model, the fluxes representing the C4 cycle are a priori constrained to the cell types (Gomes de Oliveira Dal'Molin et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gomes de Oliveira Dal'Molin et al., 2011.

claim: In the Mallmann model, the C4 fluxes are induced by activating flux through PEPC (Mallmann et al., 2014).
source: in the Mallmann model, the C4 fluxes are induced by activating flux through PEPC (Mallmann et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mallmann et al., 2014.

claim: The C4 cycle evolves from its ancestral metabolic state C3 photosynthesis along a sequence of stages (Sage, 2004; Bräutigam and Gowik, 2016).
source: Schematic models suggest that the C4 cycle evolves from its ancestral metabolic state C3 photosynthesis along a sequence of stages (summarised in Sage, 2004; Bräutigam and Gowik, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sage, 2004 and Bräutigam and Gowik, 2016.

claim: In the presence of tight vein spacing and of photosynthetically active bundle sheath cells (i.e. Kranz anatomy), a key intermediate in which the process of photorespiration is divided between cell types is thought to evolve (Monson, 1999; Sage et al., 2012; Heckmann et al., 2013; Bauwe, 2010).
source: In the presence of tight vein spacing and of photosynthetically active bundle sheath cells (i.e. Kranz anatomy), a key intermediate in which the process of photorespiration is divided between cell types is thought to evolve (Monson, 1999; Sage et al., 2012; Heckmann et al., 2013; Bauwe, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Monson, 1999; Sage et al., 2012; Heckmann et al., 2013; and Bauwe, 2010.

claim: The metabolic fluxes in the photorespiratory intermediate suggest an immediate path towards C4 photosynthesis (Mallmann et al., 2014; Bräutigam and Gowik, 2016).
source: The metabolic fluxes in this intermediate suggest an immediate path towards C4 photosynthesis (Mallmann et al., 2014; Bräutigam and Gowik, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mallmann et al., 2014 and Bräutigam and Gowik, 2016.

claim: Heckmann et al. (2013) built a kinetic model in which the complex C4 cycle was represented by a single enzyme, PEPC.
source: (Heckmann et al., 2013) built a kinetic model in which the complex C4 cycle was represented by a single enzyme, PEPC.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Heckmann et al., 2013.

claim: Assuming carbon assimilation as a proxy for fitness, the Heckmann et al. model showed that the evolution from a C3 progenitor species with Kranz-type anatomy towards C4 photosynthesis occurs in modular, individually adaptive steps on a Mount Fuji fitness landscape.
source: Assuming carbon assimilation as a proxy for fitness, the model showed that the evolution from a C3 progenitor species with Kranz-type anatomy towards C4 photosynthesis occurs in modular, individually adaptive steps on a Mount Fuji fitness landscape.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Heckmann et al., 2013 in the preceding sentence.

claim: It is frequently assumed that evolution of C4 photosynthesis requires water limitation (Bräutigam and Gowik, 2016; Heckmann et al., 2013; Mallmann et al., 2014).
source: It is frequently assumed that evolution of C4 photosynthesis requires water limitation (Bräutigam and Gowik, 2016; Heckmann et al., 2013; Mallmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bräutigam and Gowik, 2016; Heckmann et al., 2013; and Mallmann et al., 2014.

claim: Ecophysiological research showed that C4 can likely evolve in wet habitats (Osborne and Freckleton, 2009; Lundgren and Christin, 2017).
source: However, ecophysiological research showed that C4 can likely evolve in wet habitats (Osborne and Freckleton, 2009; Lundgren and Christin, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Osborne and Freckleton, 2009 and Lundgren and Christin, 2017.

claim: The curated Arabidopsis core model is based on the Arabidopsis core model (Arnold and Nikoloski, 2014).
source: For reconstruction of the C3 metabolic map we curated the Arabidopsis core model (Arnold and Nikoloski, 2014) manually (Table 1) to represent the metabolism of a mesophyll cell in a mature photosynthetically active leaf of a C3 plant
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Arnold and Nikoloski, 2014.

claim: The Arabidopsis core model is a bottom-up-assembled, large-scale model relying solely on Arabidopsis-specific annotations and the inclusion of only manually curated reactions of the primary metabolism.
source: The Arabidopsis core model is a bottom-up-assembled, large-scale model relying solely on Arabidopsis-specific annotations and the inclusion of only manually curated reactions of the primary metabolism.
evidence: This is a description of the Arabidopsis core model from Arnold and Nikoloski, 2014.

claim: The Arabidopsis core model is accurate with respect to mass and energy conservation, allowing optimal nutrient utilisation and biochemically sound predictions (Arnold and Nikoloski, 2014).
source: The Arabidopsis core model is accurate with respect to mass and energy conservation, allowing optimal nutrient utilisation and biochemically sound predictions (Arnold and Nikoloski, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Arnold and Nikoloski, 2014.

claim: The one-cell model comprises in total 413 metabolites and 572 reactions, whereof 139 are internal transporters, 90 are export and eight import reactions.
source: The one-cell model comprises in total 413 metabolites and 572 reactions, whereof 139 are internal transporters, 90 are export and eight import reactions (see also below), which are involved in 59 subsystems.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model composition.

claim: The one-cell model requires a photosynthetic photon flux density (PPFD) of 193.7 μmol/(m2s).
source: The one-cell model requires a photosynthetic photon flux density (PPFD) of 193.7 μmol/(m2s) (Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about model predictions shown in Table 2.

claim: The one-cell model takes up 0.8 μmol/(m2s) of NO3-.
source: The one-cell model takes up the maximal amount of CO2 to produce the maximum amount of phloem sap, as well as 0.8 μmol/(m2s) of NO3-
evidence: This is a direct statement about model predictions.

claim: The one-cell model takes up 18.2 μmol/(m2s) of H2O.
source: as well as 0.8 μmol/(m2s) of NO3- and 18.2 μmol/(m2s) of H2O.
evidence: This is a direct statement about model predictions.

claim: The flux of sucrose predicted by the one-cell model is 0.5 μmol/(m2s).
source: According to the assumed ratio of sucrose and amino acids in the phloem sap, the flux of sucrose predicted by the model is 0.5 μmol/(m2s)
evidence: This is a direct statement about model predictions.

claim: The flux of amino acids predicted by the one-cell model is 0.3 μmol/(m2s).
source: the flux of sucrose predicted by the model is 0.5 μmol/(m2s) and of amino acids 0.3 μmol/(m2s).
evidence: This is a direct statement about model predictions.

claim: The rate of oxygen supply by the one-cell model network is 20.9 μmol/(m2s).
source: The rate of oxygen supply by the network is 20.9 μmol/(m2s).
evidence: This is a direct statement about model predictions.

claim: The CO2 uptake rate and the phloem sap output have a positive linear relationship.
source: The CO2 uptake rate and the phloem sap output have a positive linear relationship, see Figure 1—figure supplement 1(A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1(A).

claim: The PPFD and phloem sap output have a positive linear relationship in the range of 100 μmol/(m2s)–200 μmol/(m2s).
source: The same is true for the correlation of the PPFD and phloem sap output in the range of 100 μmol/(m2s)–200 μmol/(m2s), see Figure 1—figure supplement 1(B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1(B).

claim: Above 200 μmol/(m2s) PPFD, the CO2 uptake rate acts as a limiting factor restricting the increase of phloem sap production.
source: Above 200 μmol/(m2s), the CO2 uptake rate acts as a limiting factor restricting the increase of phloem sap production.
evidence: This is an inference from the model predictions shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1(B).

claim: If either the PPFD or the CO2 uptake rate is zero, the phloem sap cannot be produced.
source: If either the PPFD or the CO2 uptake rate is zero, the phloem sap cannot be produced, compare Figure 1—figure supplement 1(A) and (B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1(A) and (B).

claim: Most of the metabolic processes use ATP/ADP as main energy equivalent (60%), followed by NADP/NADPH (37.5%) and NAD/NADH (2.4%).
source: Most of the metabolic processes use ATP/ADP as main energy equivalent (60%), followed by NADP/NADPH (37.5%) and NAD/NADH (2.4%), see Figure 1—figure supplement 2(D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2(D).

claim: Nearly all ATP is produced by the light reactions (97.2%) and consumed by the reductive pentose phosphate cycle (94.1%).
source: Nearly all ATP is produced by the light reactions (97.2%) and consumed by the reductive pentose phosphate cycle (94.1%), see Figure 1—figure supplement 2(A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2(A).

claim: The oxidative phosphorylation produces only 1% of ATP.
source: The oxidative phosphorylation produces only (1%) of ATP.
evidence: This is a direct statement about model predictions.

claim: The maintenance cost for protein synthesis and degradation makeup 28% of the respiratory ATP produced by the oxidative phosphorylation.
source: In proportion, the maintenance cost for protein synthesis and degradation makeup 28% of the respiratory ATP produced by the oxidative phosphorylation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2(E)).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2(E).

claim: Nearly all NADPH is produced by the light reaction (98.9%), which is consumed by the reductive pentose-phosphate cycle (98.3%).
source: Similarly, nearly all NADPH is produced by the light reaction (98.9%), which is consumed by the reductive pentose-phosphate cycle (98.3%) as well (Figure 1—figure supplement 2(B)).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2(B).

claim: The canonical glycolysis and photorespiration produce nearly equal amounts of NADH, 45% and 47.7%.
source: The canonical glycolysis and photorespiration produce nearly equal amounts of NADH, 45% and 47.7%
evidence: This is a direct statement about model predictions.

claim: Pyruvate dehydrogenase activity produces 6.85% of NADH.
source: significantly less NADH is produced through the pyruvate dehydrogenase activity 6.85%.
evidence: This is a direct statement about model predictions.

claim: Nitrate assimilation (45%), glutamate biosynthesis (47.7%), glyoxylate cycle (21.6%) and alternative respiration (11.8%) consume the produced NADH.
source: Nitrate assimilation (45%), glutamate biosynthesis (47.7%), glyoxylate cycle (21.6%) and alternative respiration (11.8%) consume the produced NADH (Figure 1—figure supplement 2(C)).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2(C).

claim: The model identifies resource limitation in conjunction with high photorespiratory flux as a selective pressure relevant to the evolution of C4.
source: The model thus identifies resource limitation in conjunction with high photorespiratory flux as a selective pressure relevant to the evolution of C4.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model predictions.

claim: The model predicts that light availability and distribution play a role in guiding the evolutionary choice of possible decarboxylation enzymes.
source: It also predicts that light availability and distribution play a role in guiding the evolutionary choice of possible decarboxylation enzymes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model predictions.

claim: At low photorespiratory levels, flux through PEPC is barely detectable.
source: At low photorespiratory levels, flux through PEPC is barely detectable (Figure 3(A)).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3(A).

claim: If photorespiration increases to moderate levels, flux through PEPC can be predicted and increases to 40 μmol/(m2s) for high photorespiratory fluxes.
source: If photorespiration increases to moderate levels, flux through PEPC can be predicted and increases to 40 μmol/(m2s), that is all CO2 is funnelled through PEPC, for high photorespiratory fluxes.
evidence: This is a direct statement about model predictions shown in Figure 3(A).

claim: At low to intermediate levels of photorespiratory flux, glycine decarboxylase complex activity is predicted to shuttle CO2 to the bundle sheath at up to 4.7 μmol/(m2s).
source: At low to intermediate levels of photorespiratory flux, glycine decarboxylase complex activity is predicted to shuttle CO2 to the bundle sheath at up to 4.7 μmol/(m2s).
evidence: This is a direct statement about model predictions.

claim: Decarboxylation of C4 acids is initially mostly mediated by PEP-CK and is largely taken over by NADP-ME at high fluxes through photorespiration.
source: Decarboxylation of C4 acids is initially mostly mediated by PEP-CK and is largely taken over by NADP-ME at high fluxes through photorespiration.
evidence: This is a direct statement about model predictions shown in Figure 3(B).

claim: Flux through NAD-ME is very low under all photorespiration levels.
source: Flux through NAD-ME is very low under all photorespiration levels.
evidence: This is a direct statement about model predictions shown in Figure 3(B).

claim: At low photorespiratory flux, both the Rubiscos in mesophyll and bundle sheath are active.
source: At low photorespiratory flux, both the Rubiscos in mesophyll and bundle sheath are active.
evidence: This is a direct statement about model predictions shown in Figure 3(C).

claim: At low rates of photorespiration when PEPC is barely active, the only flux towards the bundle sheath is CO2 diffusion with no fluxes towards the mesophyll.
source: At low rates of photorespiration when PEPC is barely active, the only flux towards the bundle sheath is CO2 diffusion (Figure 3(E)) with no fluxes towards the mesophyll (Figure 3(F)).

claim: In the intermediate phase glycolate and glycerate are predicted to be transported and a low-level C4 cycle dependent on the transport of aspartate, malate, PEP and alanine operates.
source: In the intermediate phase glycolate and glycerate are predicted to be transported and a low-level C4 cycle dependent on the transport of aspartate, malate, PEP and alanine operates (Figure 3(E) and (F)).

claim: In case of high photorespiratory rates, the exchange between mesophyll and bundle sheath is mainly carried by malate and pyruvate.
source: In case of high photorespiratory rates, the exchange between mesophyll and bundle sheath is mainly carried by malate and pyruvate (Figure 3(E) and (F)).

claim: Evolution of C4 photosynthesis with NADP-ME as the major decarboxylation enzyme is predicted if the photorespiratory flux is high and model optimised for minimal total flux.
source: Evolution of C4 photosynthesis with NADP-ME as the major decarboxylation enzyme is predicted if the photorespiratory flux is high and model optimised for minimal total flux, in other words, resource limitation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model predictions.

claim: Among the known independent evolutionary events leading to C4 photosynthesis, 20 are towards NAD-ME while 21 occurred towards NADP-ME (Sage, 2004).
source: Among the known independent evolutionary events leading to C4 photosynthesis, 20 are towards NAD-ME while 21 occurred towards NADP-ME (Sage, 2004).

source: PEP-CK is dominant or at least co-dominant only in Panicum maximum (Bräutigam et al., 2014), Alloteropsis semialata semialata (Christin et al., 2012), and in the Chloridoideae (Sage, 2004).

claim: The flux distribution in the mesophyll is identical for three predicted C4 cycles of the decarboxylation enzymes.
source: While the flux distribution in the mesophyll is identical for three predicted C4 cycles of the decarboxylation enzymes, it is diverse in the bundle sheath due to the different localisation of the decarboxylation and related transport processes, see Figure 4.

claim: The flux distribution is diverse in the bundle sheath due to the different localisation of the decarboxylation and related transport processes.
source: it is diverse in the bundle sheath due to the different localisation of the decarboxylation and related transport processes, see Figure 4.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: All of the decarboxylation enzymes use the malate/pyruvate shuttle.

claim: In the case of NAD-ME and PEP-CK, the two-cell model also predicts a supplementary flux through the aspartate/alanine shuttle.
source: In the case of NAD-ME and PEP-CK, the two-cell model also predicts a supplementary flux through the aspartate/alanine shuttle.
evidence: This is a direct statement about model predictions shown in Figure 4.

claim: For the NAD-ME and PEP-CK types, changes in the near-optimal space were observed for the transfer acids malate, aspartate, pyruvate and alanine.
source: For the NAD-ME and PEP-CK types, changes in the near-optimal space were observed for the transfer acids malate, aspartate, pyruvate and alanine.

source: For the NADP-ME type, FVA identifies only minor variation (Figure 5).

claim: Limiting water or CO2 uptake into the model resulted in overall reduced flux towards the phloem output but reactions were predicted to occur in the same proportions as predicted for unlimited uptake.

claim: Under light limitation, if the total PPFD is lower than 400 μmol/(m2s), the CO2 uptake rate is reduced, leading to a decreased activity of the decarboxylation enzymes.

claim: PEP-CK is used in the optimal solutions active under light-limiting conditions.
source: PEP-CK is used in the optimal solutions active under light-limiting conditions (Figure 6(B)).

claim: Under limiting light conditions, photon distribution with a higher proportion in the bundle sheath shifts decarboxylation towards NADP-ME but only to up to 26%.
source: Under limiting light conditions, photon distribution with a higher proportion in the bundle sheath shifts decarboxylation towards NADP-ME but only to up to 26%.

claim: Under non-limiting conditions, the distribution of light availability determines the optimal decarboxylation enzyme.
source: Under non-limiting conditions, the distribution of light availability determines the optimal decarboxylation enzyme.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model predictions shown in Figure 6(B).

claim: NADP-ME is the preferred decarboxylation enzyme with supplemental contributions by PEP-CK if light availability is near the threshold of 400 μmol/(m2s) or if at least twice as many photons are absorbed by the mesophyll.
source: NADP-ME is the preferred decarboxylation enzyme with supplemental contributions by PEP-CK if light availability is near the threshold of 400 μmol/(m2s) or if at least twice as many photons are absorbed by the mesophyll.
evidence: This is a direct statement about model predictions shown in Figure 6(B).

claim: Excess light availability and a higher proportion of photons reaching the bundle sheath leads to optimal solutions which favour PEP-CK as the decarboxylation enzyme.
source: Excess light availability and a higher proportion of photons reaching the bundle sheath leads to optimal solutions which favour PEP-CK as the decarboxylation enzyme.
evidence: This is a direct statement about model predictions shown in Figure 6(B).

claim: In the case of very high light availability and an abrupt shift towards the bundle sheath, NAD-ME becomes the optimal solution.
source: In the case of very high light availability and an abrupt shift towards the bundle sheath, NAD-ME becomes the optimal solution (Figure 6(B)).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6(B).

claim: NAD-ME is the least favourable enzyme overall, only low activity is predicted under extreme light conditions, where the bundle sheath absorbs equal or more photons than the mesophyll.
source: NAD-ME is the least favourable enzyme overall, only low activity is predicted under extreme light conditions, where the bundle sheath absorbs equal or more photons than the mesophyll (Figure 6(B)).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6(B).

claim: PEP-CK complements the activity of NADP-ME and NAD-ME to 100% in many conditions, meaning the two-cell model also predicts the co-existence of PEP-CK/NADP-ME and PEP-CK/NAD-ME mode.
source: PEP-CK complements the activity of NADP-ME and NAD-ME to 100% in many conditions, meaning the two-cell model also predicts the co-existence of PEP-CK/NADP-ME and PEP-CK/NAD-ME mode, while the flux distribution indicates no parallel use of NAD-ME and NADP-ME, compare Figure 6(B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6(B).

claim: The flux distribution indicates no parallel use of NAD-ME and NADP-ME.
source: while the flux distribution indicates no parallel use of NAD-ME and NADP-ME, compare Figure 6(B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6(B).

claim: Higher proportions of malate exchange foster the use of NADP-ME.

source: In contrast, higher portions of aspartate exchange foster the use of PEP-CK (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).

claim: All of the models of C4 evolution (Monson, 1999; Bauwe, 2010; Sage et al., 2012; Heckmann et al., 2013; Williams et al., 2013) predict that the establishment of a photorespiratory CO2 pump is an essential intermediate step towards the C4 cycle.
